<reason>A close, high-quality clash. CON's strongest move was to shift the debate from security to delivery by pointing to Germany/Switzerland as work-linked systems with backstops, then pressing queues versus wallet rationing. But that defense repeatedly required state-guaranteed detachment of access from job status (subsidized continuation, capped cost-sharing, unemployment-funded contributions), which is precisely the tie the motion condemns. PRO exploited this consistently and crystallized it with the floor/net distinction, explaining why a post-loss application-based net still leaves job lock, mid-treatment churn, and recession synchronization in the gap. PRO's efficiency/administrative-waste and job-lock arguments went largely unanswered, and PRO gave a plausible answer (US as the paradigm CON-side case) to CON's falsifiability challenge. CON landed real hits—Canada's queues persisting despite visibility, the zero-income German worker having near-zero exposure, and a fair "expensive way to buy portability" weighing—and PRO's closing did not fully answer the "visible for decades, still there" point. PRO also misleadingly claimed its questions went "unanswered" before CON had a turn to answer, and CON's Rebuttal 2 was clipped. On balance PRO kept the motion's actual dividing line in view and had more unrebutted live routes, giving it a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Germany exchange: CON's [B2.1]-[B2.3] argued a public backstop doesn't make a system single-payer and that PRO's security case no longer distinguishes the options; PRO's [A2.1]/[A4.1]/[A5.2] countered that every safeguard CON relies on is the state untying access from work, so CON's defense works only by adopting PRO's principle through extra intermediaries. This exchange defined the debate and PRO came out slightly ahead on it.</best_rebuttal>
